Page 3
ASQL1 - Advanced joins and grain control
1. Why it matters
The most dangerous SQL join errors often run successfully and produce believable totals. If a one-to-many or many-to-many
relationship
was not expected, revenue or counts can multiply silently.
2. What you are learning
State row grain and key/cardinality on both sides before joining. Predict output grain, select the join kind deliberately, surface
unmatched rows
and prove whether any fan-out is expected.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
Course 1 SELECT/WHERE/GROUP BY and basic INNER/LEFT JOIN. C2-00 grain language should be familiar.
4. Picture it in your head
Row-multiplication ledger: Before a join, write the row grain on the left and right. Predict how many matches each key
can create. If a one-row order meets three item rows, the ledger says three output rows unless you first aggregate to
order grain.
5. New words before we use them
Cardinality: How many matching rows may exist on each side of a relationship. Fan-out: Unexpected row multiplication after a
join. Orphan key: A
foreign/business key with no matching parent/master row.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED VIDEO: Alex The Analyst - Learn SQL Beginner to Advanced in Under 4 Hours. 51:10-1:08:03.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OT1RErkfLNQ
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Joins Between Tables. Join concepts.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-join.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Declare orders = one row per order_id. Declare order_items = one row per order_id + line_id.
- Do not join order-level order_value to item rows and then SUM(order_value), because each order value would repeat once
per item.
- First aggregate line items to the order grain: WITH line_totals AS (SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity*unit_price) AS
line_value FROM
- order_items GROUP BY order_id).
- Join orders to line_totals on order_id. Predict one output row per order.
- Validate with COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), unmatched order_ids, and an independent total. If rows > distinct
orders, investigate
- instead of adding DISTINCT.
8. What you should see / be able to say
One row per intended order with no unexplained multiplication and a saved orphan/fan-out check.
9. Why it worked
The many-side table was reduced to the required output grain before the join, so the join contract matched the intended
result. Professional upgrade:
Production analytical SQL usually documents expected cardinality and validates it. A reviewer should be able to see why row
count changed and whether that
change was intended.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 4
1. Joining before writing the two row-grain sentences. | 2. Using DISTINCT to hide fan-out. | 3. Using INNER JOIN when
unmatched source rows
must remain visible. | 4. Validating only the final total without row/key checks.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Run each table alone. Record rows and distinct business keys. Join only keys first. Compare row count before/after. List
duplicates and orphans.
Repair the first stage where predicted grain breaks. Save the genuine attempt before protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: customers, subscriptions and invoice_lines. Produce one row per subscription with billed value. One customer
has multiple subscriptions
and one invoice references a missing subscription.
13. Validate your result
State input/output grain, show distinct-key parity, list unmatched keys, and reconcile billed value independently.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why a join can be syntactically correct and analytically wrong.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Save the query and validation first. Then review; close it and retry on a different ticket-event/customer case.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Runnable SQL + grain/cardinality note + unmatched check + row/total reconciliation + explain-back. VIDEO SUPPORT: Alex
The Analyst -
51:10-1:08:03 joins https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-join.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL2.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 5
ASQL2 - Subqueries and derived tables
1. Why it matters
Nested SQL becomes confusing when the inner query has no clear purpose or grain. A useful subquery should simplify one
logical stage
and make the final question easier to validate.
2. What you are learning
Use scalar, IN/EXISTS and derived-table subqueries appropriately; identify inner result shape; alias derived tables; avoid
accidental correlated
work when a simpler staged query will do.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
ASQL1 joins and GROUP BY/aggregates.
4. Picture it in your head
Question inside a question: A subquery is a smaller answer box used by a larger question. First prove the inner result
has the grain and columns the outer query expects; then decide whether it belongs in WHERE, FROM, or a scalar
expression.
5. New words before we use them
Scalar subquery: A subquery expected to return one value. Derived table: A subquery in FROM treated like a temporary
result for that SELECT. Correlated
subquery: A subquery that refers to values from the outer query and may be evaluated in relation to each outer row.
6. Watch / visual source
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - SELECT. Subselect/SELECT behavior.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Stage 1: create one row per customer with SUM(order_value) after the approved status filter.
- Inspect that stage alone. Its grain is one row per customer.
- Stage 2: compute AVG(revenue) from that customer-level result. This must return one scalar value.
- Outer query filters customer rows where revenue > the scalar average.
- Validate by saving the scalar average and checking the minimum returned revenue is greater than it.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A nested query where every inner result has a stated shape and can be run independently for debugging.
9. Why it worked
The average is computed at customer grain instead of order grain, so the business question and denominator align.
Professional upgrade: Choose
subqueries for compact local logic; choose CTEs when named stages improve review and validation. Maintainability matters
more than showing nesting skill.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Computing average order value when the question says average customer revenue. | 2. Writing a scalar subquery that
returns multiple rows. |
3. Nesting before testing the inner result. | 4. Using subqueries when named CTE stages would be clearer.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Run the deepest subquery alone. Write its expected columns, row count and grain. Fix it before adding the next level. Save
the genuine attempt before
protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 6
Fresh case: return products whose monthly revenue is above the average monthly product revenue for the same period.
13. Validate your result
Record the inner average, count returned rows and prove every returned value passes the threshold.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain a derived table as a temporary result inside one query without calling it a permanent table.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry uses EXISTS to find customers with at least one qualifying event.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Nested SQL + inner-result screenshots/text + independent threshold check + explain-back. VIDEO: intentionally book-led for
this lesson
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL3.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 7
ASQL3 - CTEs and readable query architecture
1. Why it matters
A 70-line query with repeated filters can be correct today and dangerous tomorrow. Named stages let another analyst test
each
transformation and prevent business rules from drifting across repeated fragments.
2. What you are learning
Use WITH CTEs to name logical stages, centralize filters, document stage grain and validate intermediate outputs.
Understand that CTEs are
query expressions, not automatically stored tables.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
ASQL2 subqueries and ASQL1 grain control.
4. Picture it in your head
Labeled pipeline stages: A CTE chain is a sequence of named worktables: scope -> clean -> aggregate -> compare ->
final. Each stage should have one grain and one purpose, so you can validate it before moving on.
5. New words before we use them
CTE: Common Table Expression: a named query result defined in a WITH clause for use in the statement. Stage grain: The
row meaning produced by one
CTE stage. Materialization: Whether PostgreSQL stores/evaluates a CTE result separately versus integrating it into planning;
behavior can matter for
performance.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED VIDEO: Alex The Analyst - CTE chapter. 1:58:55-2:09:06.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OT1RErkfLNQ
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - WITH Queries. CTE behavior.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- base: filter source rows once using the approved business rule.
- customer_month: aggregate base to one row per customer + month.
- validated: add only checks or classifications needed before final output; do not hide bad rows.
- final SELECT: choose the business-facing columns and deterministic ORDER BY.
- Run each CTE by temporarily selecting from it to verify row count, distinct keys and control totals.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A query whose stages have meaningful names and whose stage grain can be explained independently.
9. Why it worked
Repeated logic became one controlled stage, making drift and debugging easier to detect. Professional upgrade: In
production SQL, stage names often
communicate contracts: source_scope, deduped, enriched, customer_day, validated, final. Keep one responsibility per stage
where practical.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Using CTE names like a,b,c that reveal nothing. | 2. Repeating slightly different status filters in multiple CTEs. | 3.
Assuming every CTE
improves performance. | 4. Leaving validation only in comments without runnable queries.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 8
Collapse the query to base only. Add one CTE at a time. After each addition, run a control SELECT from that CTE. Save the
genuine attempt before
protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: build eligible_orders -> customer_week -> ranked_customer_week -> final_exception_report.
13. Validate your result
For every stage save rows, distinct business keys and one control total appropriate to the grain.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why CTEs improve reviewability even when they do not make the query faster.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry restructures a nested query into named stages.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
CTE query + stage-grain table + stage controls + explain-back. VIDEO SUPPORT: Alex The Analyst - 1:58:55-2:09:06 CTEs
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-with.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL4.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 9
ASQL4 - Window functions fundamentals
1. Why it matters
GROUP BY collapses rows. Many business questions need a group calculation while still keeping each row - for example
each order plus
the customer's total or department average.
2. What you are learning
Recognize when a window function is needed; use OVER, PARTITION BY and ORDER BY; explain why row identity is
retained; filter window
results through a later query stage when necessary.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
Aggregates and ASQL3 staged queries.
4. Picture it in your head
Keep the rows, add a lens: GROUP BY collapses rows; a window function keeps the underlying rows and adds a
calculated lens across related rows. State the partition and order before choosing the window expression.
5. New words before we use them
Window function: A calculation across related rows that keeps the individual output rows. PARTITION BY: Divides result rows
into groups for the window
calculation. OVER: Marks the function as a window calculation and defines its window.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED VIDEO: Alex The Analyst - Window Functions chapter. 1:45:58-1:58:54.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OT1RErkfLNQ
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Window Functions tutorial. Window mental model.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-window.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Start with eligible orders at one row per order.
- Add SUM(order_value) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_revenue.
- Compare output row count to input row count; it should remain one row per eligible order.
- Pick one customer and independently GROUP BY customer_id to confirm the repeated customer_revenue value.
- If you need top rows based on a window result, calculate the window in a subquery/CTE and filter in the outer SELECT.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Window result added without collapsing order rows, with a saved independent grouped check.
9. Why it worked
OVER changes the aggregate from row-collapsing behavior to a calculation over a defined set while rows retain identity.
Professional upgrade: Window
functions are excellent for analytical comparisons, but partition, order and frame are part of the business definition and should
be reviewed like any other
metric logic.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Expecting window SUM to reduce rows. | 2. Putting window functions directly in WHERE. | 3. Using PARTITION BY when
the business
question needs the whole result set. | 4. Forgetting that window ORDER BY affects calculation order, not necessarily final
display order.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Complete the matching course task and preserve your evidence before moving on.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 10
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: show every ticket with team average resolution time while keeping one row per ticket.
13. Validate your result
Base/output rows equal; one team's window value matches independent GROUP BY result.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain GROUP BY versus a window function using 'collapse rows' versus 'keep rows'.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry uses each transaction plus account-level total.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Runnable window SQL + base/output row parity + independent partition check + explain-back. VIDEO SUPPORT: Alex The
window functions https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-window.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL5.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 11
ASQL5 - Ranking, partitions and running calculations
1. Why it matters
Top-N and running totals look simple until ties or duplicate timestamps appear. ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK
answer
different questions, and default window frames can surprise you.
2. What you are learning
Choose ranking function based on tie policy; define deterministic ordering; distinguish partition from frame; write explicit
ROWS frames for
running calculations when needed.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
ASQL4 window basics.
4. Picture it in your head
Resettable race track: PARTITION BY creates separate tracks; ORDER BY decides the race order inside each track;
ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK decide how positions behave when values tie. A running calculation also needs
an explicit frame.
5. New words before we use them
ROW_NUMBER: Unique sequential number according to the specified window order. RANK: Ranking with gaps after ties.
DENSE_RANK: Ranking without
gaps after ties. Frame: The subset of rows within the window used for a particular calculation.
6. Watch / visual source
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Window Functions. Ranking/frame functions.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- For top order value per customer, decide tie policy before picking ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK.
- Add a deterministic tie-breaker such as order_id after order_value if exactly one row must win.
- For running spend, order by order_date, order_id and write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW explicitly.
- Select one customer and manually sort their orders to verify the first three running totals.
- Document whether two equal order values should share rank or one must be chosen deterministically.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Ranking and running-total logic matches a written tie/frame policy.
9. Why it worked
The business rule controls ranking and window frame instead of relying on defaults. Professional upgrade: Stable analytical
outputs use deterministic sort
keys. If the decision requires exactly N rows, document how ties are broken.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Using ROW_NUMBER when ties should share a rank. | 2. Ordering by a non-unique timestamp without tie-breaker. | 3.
Assuming default
frame always means 'rows so far'. | 4. Using final ORDER BY as if it changed window calculation order.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Create a tiny 5-row example with an intentional tie. Compare ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK. Then test the frame on
the same rows. Save the
genuine attempt before protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 12
Fresh case: top two products per region by revenue plus cumulative monthly revenue within region.
13. Validate your result
Check tie case explicitly and manually recompute one partition's running values.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why a ranking function choice is a business rule, not only syntax.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry uses employee performance scores with deliberate ties.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Ranking SQL + tie policy + explicit frame + manual partition check + explain-back. VIDEO: intentionally book-led for this
lesson
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL6.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 13
ASQL6 - LAG, LEAD and time-based comparisons
1. Why it matters
Month-over-month or event-to-event comparison is wrong if the rows are not first reduced to the correct time grain and
ordered
deterministically.
2. What you are learning
Use LAG/LEAD after defining entity and time grain; handle the first/last row; distinguish missing period from zero; calculate
changes only after
validating ordering and continuity.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
ASQL5 window ordering and ASQL8-style typed dates will reinforce this lesson.
4. Picture it in your head
Time-neighbor ruler: LAG and LEAD let each row look to a defined neighbor in an ordered series. The ruler is
meaningful only when the time grain is complete and the ordering key is deterministic; missing periods do not
magically appear.
5. New words before we use them
LAG: Returns a value from a previous row in the window ordering. LEAD: Returns a value from a following row in the window
ordering. Time grain: The time
unit represented by one row, such as one row per month.
6. Watch / visual source
OPTIONAL VIDEO: Alex The Analyst - Window Functions chapter. 1:45:58-1:58:54.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OT1RErkfLNQ
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Window Functions. LAG/LEAD.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- First aggregate eligible orders to one row per month using date_trunc('month', order_date).
- Apply LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) to the monthly result, not raw order rows.
- Compute absolute change and, only when denominator policy is defined, percentage change.
- Check the first month: prior_revenue should be NULL because no earlier row exists.
- Detect whether a missing calendar month is absent from the data. Missing row is not the same as a zero-revenue month.
8. What you should see / be able to say
One row per month with prior value/change and an explicit policy for first/missing periods.
9. Why it worked
The time series is normalized to month grain before row-to-row comparison. Professional upgrade: For operational time
series, a calendar/date spine may be
needed to represent missing periods explicitly. That deeper modeling appears later; here you must at least detect the
difference.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Using LAG on unsummarized order rows for monthly change. | 2. Treating NULL prior value as zero automatically. | 3.
Ignoring missing
months. | 4. Ordering by formatted month text instead of typed time.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Run the monthly CTE alone. Confirm one row per period and chronological order. Only then add LAG/LEAD. Save the
genuine attempt before
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 14
protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: weekly support volume by team with previous-week comparison; one week is missing for one team.
13. Validate your result
Manually check two adjacent periods and explicitly flag the missing-period condition.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why LAG does not know what 'previous month' means unless your row set and order make it true.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry compares next scheduled appointment per patient with LEAD.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Time-grain query + LAG/LEAD + missing-period check + manual comparison + explain-back. VIDEO SUPPORT: Alex The
optional window visual; LAG/LEAD taught in-book https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html After
saving evidence, continue to
ASQL7.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 15
ASQL7 - Conditional aggregation and advanced KPI queries
1. Why it matters
A KPI query can return a neat percentage while numerator and denominator use different populations. Conditional
aggregation must
implement the metric contract visibly.
2. What you are learning
Use CASE and PostgreSQL FILTER for conditional counts/sums; separate numerator and denominator; use NULLIF for
defined
zero-denominator behavior; reconcile KPI components independently.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
C2-00 metric contracts, aggregates, ASQL1 grain.
4. Picture it in your head
One scan, many buckets: Conditional aggregation sends each input row into named KPI buckets using CASE/FILTER
rules, then aggregates once. Write each numerator and denominator rule in words before encoding it.
5. New words before we use them
Conditional aggregation: Aggregating only rows that satisfy a condition, often through CASE or FILTER. FILTER clause:
PostgreSQL syntax that applies a
WHERE-like condition to one aggregate. NULLIF: Returns NULL when two expressions are equal; often used to avoid
division by zero after the business rule
is defined.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED VIDEO: Alex The Analyst - CASE Statements chapter. 1:26:39-1:35:15.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OT1RErkfLNQ
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Aggregate Functions. Aggregate behavior.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-aggregate.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Write the metric contract first: numerator = completed eligible orders; denominator = all eligible non-test orders.
- Use COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status='completed') for numerator when PostgreSQL is the target dialect.
- Build denominator separately with its own eligible-population filter; do not assume COUNT(*) is correct.
- Compute rate using numerator::numeric / NULLIF(denominator,0) only after zero-population behavior is agreed.
- Reconcile numerator and denominator for one region with independent WHERE queries.
8. What you should see / be able to say
KPI output whose components can be inspected and independently recomputed.
9. Why it worked
Business definitions stay visible in the aggregate expressions instead of being hidden in a final ratio. Professional upgrade: In
reviewed SQL, metric
components are often named in a CTE so definitions can be tested and reused. Keep business labels close to the exact filters
they mean.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Different filters on numerator and denominator by accident. | 2. ELSE NULL versus ELSE 0 confusion without
understanding aggregate
behavior. | 3. IFERROR-like hiding of zero denominator. | 4. Formatting as percent before validating components.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Complete the matching course task and preserve your evidence before moving on.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 16
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: First Contact Resolution Rate by team with an exclusion for reopened-within-48-hours cases.
13. Validate your result
Independent numerator/denominator queries match output; sum of segments reconciles to overall eligible population where
appropriate.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why a percentage should be built last, not first.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry builds refund rate with a different denominator.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
KPI SQL + metric contract + component validation + explain-back. VIDEO SUPPORT: Alex The Analyst - 1:26:39-1:35:15
CASE statements
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-aggregate.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL8.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 17
ASQL8 - Date and time analysis
1. Why it matters
Text slicing and inclusive end dates often create hidden period errors. Timestamps also introduce time-zone and boundary
questions that
must be explicit.
2. What you are learning
Use typed DATE/TIMESTAMP values, half-open intervals, date_trunc/date_bin where appropriate, and explicit time-zone
assumptions. Avoid
text-based month logic.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
Basic WHERE filters; ASQL6 time-grain reasoning.
4. Picture it in your head
Half-open calendar boxes: Put timestamps into boxes such as [start, next_start). This includes the first instant and
excludes the next period boundary, avoiding 23:59:59 tricks and making month/week logic safe across timestamp
precision.
5. New words before we use them
Half-open interval: A time filter including the start and excluding the next-period boundary, such as >= Apr 1 and < May 1.
date_trunc: PostgreSQL function
that truncates a date/time value to a requested precision. Time zone: Rules used to interpret local clock time relative to
UTC/other zones.
6. Watch / visual source
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Date/Time Functions and Operators. date_trunc/date-time behavior.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-datetime.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Use order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00' AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2026-07-01 00:00:00'.
- Bucket with date_trunc('month', order_ts) after confirming the business reporting time zone.
- Do not use BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-06-30' for timestamp data unless you truly intend the end literal behavior.
- Check minimum and maximum timestamps returned and count rows exactly at a boundary in a tiny test.
- If source is timestamptz, record the reporting-zone decision before grouping by local month.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Typed, boundary-safe period logic with explicit calendar/time-zone assumptions.
9. Why it worked
The next-period exclusive boundary includes every instant in the intended period without guessing the final day's maximum
time. Professional upgrade:
Period logic belongs in metric contracts. Reporting month, operational day and UTC storage can all be different concepts.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Comparing dates stored as text. | 2. Using <= end_date with timestamp data carelessly. | 3. Grouping UTC timestamps into
local business
days without a zone decision. | 4. Formatting first, then grouping on strings.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Inspect column data type and sample minimum/maximum. Test one record at the start boundary and one at the next-period
boundary. Save the
genuine attempt before protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 18
Fresh case: analyze support events by local business day when timestamps are stored with time zone.
13. Validate your result
Boundary test rows behave as predicted; bucket count reconciles to filtered source count.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain half-open date filtering using a shop open from one boundary until the next.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry uses weekly buckets with a different reporting zone.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Typed date/time SQL + boundary tests + bucket reconciliation + explain-back. VIDEO: intentionally book-led for this lesson
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/functions-datetime.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL9.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 19
ASQL9 - Data-quality investigation with SQL
1. Why it matters
Data quality should be investigated before it contaminates a metric. SQL can turn vague suspicion into exact exception sets
that can be
counted, owned and repaired.
2. What you are learning
Write reusable checks for duplicate business keys, null required fields, orphan keys, invalid ranges, unexpected categories
and cross-table
control totals.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
ASQL1 joins/grain and basic aggregates.
4. Picture it in your head
Exception flashlight: Data-quality SQL is not trying to hide bad rows; it shines a light on duplicates, nulls, orphans,
impossible values and reconciliation breaks. Keep an exception result beside the cleaned result.
5. New words before we use them
Profiling query: A query that summarizes shape, values or exceptions to understand data quality. Required field: A field
whose missing value makes a
business process or analysis invalid. Domain rule: A rule defining valid values/ranges for a field.
6. Watch / visual source
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Table and Query Expressions. Filtering/join expressions.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Duplicate customer key: GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
- Missing required field: WHERE region IS NULL OR btrim(region)=''.
- Orphan order: LEFT JOIN customers and filter c.customer_id IS NULL.
- Invalid amount: WHERE order_value < 0 when negatives are not allowed by the contract.
- Unexpected status: compare DISTINCT status against an approved status list; save exception counts rather than silently
mapping them.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A small exception report where each quality rule has count, sample keys and business impact.
9. Why it worked
The checks target different failure classes instead of relying on one generic 'clean data' query. Professional upgrade: Quality
checks become operational
when each rule has owner, severity, expected threshold and recovery action. C2-02 focuses on query design; broader
observability comes later.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Removing duplicate rows before identifying which key is duplicated. | 2. Treating all nulls as errors. | 3. Using NOT IN
carelessly when null
semantics are not understood. | 4. Fixing source values directly without owner approval.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Choose one rule at a time: grain/key, required field, relationship, range, category. Return only exception rows and count
them. Save the genuine
attempt before protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 20
Fresh case: investigate ticket, team and customer tables containing duplicate teams, orphan customer IDs and negative
resolution hours.
13. Validate your result
Exception counts are reproducible and zero only after an approved repair; raw evidence remains preserved.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why data-quality SQL should return the bad rows, not only a green/red flag.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry uses subscription/billing quality rules.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Quality-check SQL + exception outputs + business-impact note + explain-back. VIDEO: intentionally book-led for this lesson
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-table-expressions.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL10.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 21
ASQL10 - Query debugging and validation
1. Why it matters
Changing several clauses at once can make a query appear fixed without proving which error caused the problem. Senior
debugging
isolates the first broken stage.
2. What you are learning
Classify syntax versus logic versus data-quality failures; debug stage-by-stage; compare row count/distinct keys/control
totals; build validation
queries that could catch plausible wrong answers.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
ASQL1-ASQL9; especially CTE stages and grain checks.
4. Picture it in your head
Query autopsy checkpoints: When a final total is wrong, do not stare at the last SELECT. Check source population ->
filters -> joins -> grain -> aggregation -> window -> final formatting, and stop at the first stage where a control
changes unexpectedly.
5. New words before we use them
Syntax error: The database cannot parse/execute the statement as written. Logic error: The SQL runs but answers the wrong
question. Control total: An
independently obtained count/sum used to reconcile the query result.
6. Watch / visual source
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - SELECT. Query staging/debug context.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Record the symptom: final revenue is almost exactly 2x expected.
- Run base CTE controls: rows, distinct order_id, SUM(order_value).
- Run the next join stage with the same controls. If rows and total double here, stop; later stages are not the first cause.
- Inspect right-side join key for duplicates. Do not change filters or add DISTINCT yet.
- Repair the key/cardinality cause, rerun controls from base through final, and save before/after evidence.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A debugging log identifying the first failed stage and proving the repair removed the underlying cause.
9. Why it worked
The search space shrinks because every stage has shape and total evidence. Professional upgrade: Keep small diagnostic
queries near complex analytical
SQL during development. Validation queries are part of the deliverable for important outputs.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Editing many clauses before rerunning controls. | 2. Fixing the final SELECT when the error began upstream. | 3. Using the
same final query
as its own validation. | 4. Deleting problem rows until totals match.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Return to the earliest stable stage. Add one transformation at a time and compare rows, distinct keys and one additive total.
Save the genuine attempt
before protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 22
Fresh case: a monthly customer report loses 12 customers after enrichment. Find the first stage where row count drops and
decide whether the loss is
expected.
13. Validate your result
Before/after evidence shows exactly which stage changed shape and why; final controls rerun after repair.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why 'the query runs now' is not proof that the bug is fixed.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry uses an incorrect date filter rather than a join bug.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Debug log + stage controls + root cause + repair + rerun evidence + explain-back. VIDEO: intentionally book-led for this
lesson
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL11.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 23
ASQL11 - Performance concepts: indexes, scans and EXPLAIN
1. Why it matters
Optimization before correctness can make the wrong result faster. Analysts need enough plan awareness to identify obvious
scans/row-estimate problems and communicate evidence without pretending to be database administrators.
2. What you are learning
Read basic EXPLAIN nodes/cost/estimated rows; understand sequential versus index scans conceptually; know that
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
executes the statement; compare estimated and actual rows; discuss index trade-offs.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
Correct, validated SQL from earlier lessons. Basic idea of a database index is taught here.
4. Picture it in your head
Route map before stopwatch: EXPLAIN is the planner's route map; EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds actual runtime evidence.
First ask whether the query is logically correct and selective, then inspect scans/joins/index use. A faster wrong
query is still wrong.
5. New words before we use them
Query plan: The execution strategy PostgreSQL chooses for a statement. Sequential scan: Reading table pages broadly
rather than locating rows via an
index. Index scan: Using an index to locate candidate rows. Estimate: Planner prediction such as expected rows/cost before
actual execution.
6. Watch / visual source
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Using EXPLAIN. EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Indexes. Index concepts/trade-offs.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- First prove the SELECT is correct with normal validation.
- Run EXPLAIN SELECT ... to inspect the planned access path without requesting actual execution details.
- Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) only on a safe SELECT in the practice environment and remember ANALYZE
executes it.
- Compare estimated rows to actual rows and identify the largest mismatch or expensive-looking node; do not optimize from
node names alone.
- Discuss whether an index on the filter/join key could help and what write/storage overhead it adds. Measure before and after
if the lab provides
- an index.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A short plan note naming observed scan/join type, estimate-versus-actual evidence and one measured optimization
hypothesis.
9. Why it worked
Performance reasoning comes after correctness and uses observed plan evidence rather than generic 'indexes make SQL
fast' claims. Professional upgrade:
Analysts should know when to escalate a performance issue with reproducible SQL, row counts and EXPLAIN evidence
rather than guessing at database
configuration.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 24
1. Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on unsafe modifying statements without understanding execution. | 2. Calling every
sequential scan bad. | 3.
Creating many indexes without workload evidence. | 4. Comparing timing from unrelated environments as if absolute.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Use plain EXPLAIN first. Identify top nodes, estimated rows and predicates. If safe, add ANALYZE in the lab. Compare one
change at a time. Save the
genuine attempt before protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: compare a selective date/customer filter before and after an approved practice index. Record plan and timing/row
evidence.
13. Validate your result
Query result stays identical; plan evidence saved; trade-off statement includes index maintenance/storage cost.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain why a sequential scan can sometimes be the right plan.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry examines a join query with a different selectivity pattern.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Validated query + before/after EXPLAIN evidence + result parity + trade-off + explain-back. VIDEO: intentionally book-led for
this lesson
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html After saving evidence, continue to ASQL12.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 25
ASQL12 - Maintainable production-style analytical SQL
1. Why it matters
A one-off query may answer today. A production-style analytical query must let another analyst understand the decision,
assumptions,
grain, stages, validation and how to rerun it safely.
2. What you are learning
Package analytical SQL with header contract, readable CTE stages, consistent names/formatting, deterministic output,
separate validations,
business interpretation and handoff notes.
3. Prerequisite / what you already know
All ASQL1-ASQL11.
4. Picture it in your head
Production SQL assembly line: Inputs and assumptions enter, named stages transform them, controls verify
row/money contracts, and a documented final output leaves the line. Maintainability means another analyst can rerun
and audit it without guessing.
5. New words before we use them
Deterministic output: Output whose ordering/tie behavior is explicitly controlled when order matters. Query contract: Short
documentation of decision, scope,
grain, assumptions and source tables. Handoff: Information another analyst needs to rerun, validate and modify the analysis
safely.
6. Watch / visual source
OPTIONAL VIDEO: Alex The Analyst - Data Cleaning / EDA project chapters. 2:42:46-3:32:13.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OT1RErkfLNQ
CURRENT REFERENCE: PostgreSQL 18 - Queries. Query architecture.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries.html
Return to the lesson and reproduce the SQL/control from your own practice database. Save course-task evidence, not a
screenshot of the source.
7. Follow with me once
- Header comment: decision, metric definition/version, intended final grain, source tables, period, exclusions and
assumptions.
- WITH stages: base_scope -> quality_checked -> enriched -> business_grain -> final_metrics. Use descriptive aliases.
- Final SELECT includes only decision-facing columns and deterministic ORDER BY when presentation order matters.
- Separate validation block checks row/distinct-key counts, orphans and control totals; do not hide it inside comments.
- Write a 3-5 sentence interpretation: what happened, materiality, uncertainty, recommendation and what would change it.
8. What you should see / be able to say
A runnable SQL package another analyst can review stage-by-stage and reconcile without asking what each section means.
9. Why it worked
Technical logic, business contract and evidence are packaged together instead of living in separate memory/chat fragments.
Professional upgrade:
Maintainable SQL is boring in a good way: explicit contracts, stable naming, small stages, deterministic logic, validation and
evidence. Complexity is justified
only when the business problem requires it.
10. Common beginner mistakes
1. Leaving magic dates/status values unexplained. | 2. Using SELECT * in the final output without need. | 3. No deterministic
tie/order rule. | 4.
Deleting validation queries before handoff. | 5. Writing business conclusions not supported by the query.
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 26
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
Start with the header contract and final grain. Rename each stage for one job. Add one validation per major failure mode.
Only then polish formatting.
Save the genuine attempt before protected review.
12. Now you do a small version alone
Fresh case: deliver a production-style regional service-performance query with quality exceptions, KPI output and a concise
business recommendation.
13. Validate your result
A second analyst can state source/grain/rules, run validations, reproduce final output and identify one safe modification point.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain what makes SQL 'production-style' without using line count or advanced syntax as the definition.
15. Protected review + changed fresh retry
Attempt first. Changed retry packages a different subscription-health analysis.
16. Evidence / mastery + exact next route
Final SQL file + validation section + data-quality note + interpretation + handoff + 90-second defense. VIDEO SUPPORT:
Alex The Analyst -
2:42:46-3:32:13 optional cleaning/project workflow https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries.html After saving
evidence, complete the module
mastery checklist and follow the Gate A / completion route.

masteryReview.text:
Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 1
C2_02 Module Test - Protected Review
RC4
Open only after a saved genuine attempt. Diagnose the weak competency, close this review, then prove repair on a
changed query/fixture.
ASQL1
Aggregate/validate the many side to intended output grain or use the correct grain-specific measure; prove row/distinct-key
parity instead of hiding fan-out with DISTINCT.
ASQL2
Unsafe when it can return multiple rows/columns where one value is expected, or when duplicates/NULL semantics make the
comparison ambiguous.
ASQL3
Named stages expose grain and controls so each transformation can be inspected independently; readability/validation is the
goal, not forcing physical execution order.
ASQL4
GROUP BY collapses to one row/group; a window calculation preserves row grain and adds a value computed over a
partition/order/frame.
ASQL5
State tie behavior and deterministic secondary ordering. ROW_NUMBER forces unique positions; RANK/DENSE_RANK
preserve ties differently.
ASQL6
LAG returns the previous existing row, not necessarily the previous calendar period. Build/check the period series or detect
gaps.
ASQL7
Define eligible population first, then numerator subset; denominator must not drift because of joins, NULLs or hidden status
exclusions.
ASQL8
Half-open intervals are precision-safe and non-overlapping: include start, exclude next boundary. 23:59:59 can miss
higher-precision timestamps.
ASQL9
Duplicates, orphan foreign keys, null/invalid fields, impossible values/ranges, row-count and monetary reconciliation are
common minimum checks.
ASQL10
Compare rows/distinct keys/control totals immediately before and after the first suspect stage; isolate first divergence.
ASQL11
Planner route: scans, join methods/order, estimates, index usage and costs. Runtime alone does not explain why or whether
logic is correct.
ASQL12
Clear inputs/grain/assumptions, named stages, independent controls, explicit period rules, safe performance evidence,
comments/handoff and a fresh rerun path.

Course 2A | C2_02 | Astra Parity RC4
Page 2
2. Expected reasoning path
Start with grain: sellers_raw is master-key grain (but dirty); orders is one row/order; events is one row/event. Never sum
order-level gross_value after an unconstrained event join.
Duplicate key: seller_id 5 has conflicting regions. The current Gate A order fixture happens not to use seller 5, so current
order KPIs are not changed by that conflict. That does not make arbitrary dedupe safe; document and escalate the
master-data conflict.
Orphan: order 88 / seller 999 is completed for 3253.11. If you INNER JOIN to sellers and lose it, completed value falls from

68/team5 and 85/team6 qualify. At team_id grain, each team has 1 of 10 resolved tickets = 10%; that is a tie, not a unique
worst team.
